interviewQuestions.question: Design the search ranking system for an e-commerce site.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd frame this as two chained problems, not one: retrieval, then ranking. Before either runs, query understanding needs to handle spell correction, intent classification (navigational vs transactional), and query expansion — any error here means retrieval searches for the wrong thing and ranking can't recover from it.

For retrieval, I'd combine lexical search (BM25 over an inverted index, strong for exact product names and model numbers) with embedding-based semantic retrieval (catches synonyms like 'sneakers' matching 'trainers'), merging both candidate sets.

For ranking, I'd train a learning-to-rank model on query-document interaction features specifically — the same catalog should rank completely differently for 'best running shoes' versus 'cheap running shoes,' so query-document features matter more here than in a passive feed.

For evaluation, I'd use NDCG plus human relevance judgments as ground truth, since raw click data has a built-in position bias — top results get clicked more regardless of true relevance, so any click-based signal needs a click model correcting for that, or I'd validate with an interleaving experiment.

**Testing:** whether you understand search's distinguishing feature — an explicit, interpretable query — and correctly treat click data as a biased signal rather than ground truth.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: E-commerce search ranking design

interviewQuestions.question: Why does search retrieval typically combine lexical (BM25) and embedding-based semantic search rather than picking whichever one performs better on average?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
They fail on structurally different, non-overlapping classes of query, so picking one "on average" means silently accepting whichever class of failure that choice leaves uncovered — and in search, that failure is highly visible to the user as a zero-result or bad-result page. Lexical retrieval (an inverted index scored with BM25) is fast and precise for queries where exact terms matter — a model number, a specific brand name, an exact phrase — because it directly matches the literal tokens present in the query against the literal tokens in the document. Its structural blind spot is anything paraphrased: a user searching "sneakers" gets nothing from a document that only ever says "trainers," even though they mean the same thing, because there's no shared token for BM25 to match on.

Embedding-based semantic retrieval solves exactly that blind spot — queries and documents are embedded into the same vector space where semantic similarity, not token overlap, determines closeness, so "sneakers" and "trainers" land near each other. But semantic retrieval has its own structural weakness in the other direction: it can be comparatively imprecise on queries where an exact, literal match is what the user actually wants — a specific SKU or model number needs an exact match, and a semantic embedding can retrieve "similar-sounding" items that miss the one specific product the user typed the exact identifier for.

Running both in parallel and merging candidate sets means the system covers both failure classes simultaneously rather than choosing which class of query to sacrifice — a real production trade-off that "pick the better one on average" papers over by hiding the specific queries where the chosen method fails completely.

**Testing:** whether you can name the specific, opposite failure modes of lexical and semantic retrieval, not just that combining them is standard practice.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why retrieval combines lexical and semantic search

interviewQuestions.question: Your search team wants to retrain the ranking model directly on click-through data because it's abundant and cheap, skipping the expensive human relevance judgments. What's the risk, and how would you validate whether it's safe?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The risk is training a model that optimizes for and reinforces position bias rather than true relevance, and it's dangerous specifically because it's self-reinforcing and can look like success on the very metric used to validate it. Raw click data has a built-in distortion: results at higher positions get clicked more simply because users scan top-to-bottom, regardless of whether the top result is actually most relevant. Train a new ranker directly on raw clicks and it learns to reproduce whatever the current ranking already rewards — a mediocre result at position 1 accumulates clicks purely from visibility, and the model learns "this deserves to rank highly" from that pattern, when the real signal is "this was seen first, not judged best." Deploy it and it doubles down on the current ranking's biases rather than correcting them, and every retraining cycle on the new click data reinforces the loop further.

To validate whether this is actually safe, I wouldn't check if the click-trained model matches historical clicks well — that's circular, since it's optimizing for the exact biased signal in question. I'd hold out human relevance judgments as independent ground truth specifically to check whether the model's rankings correlate with judged relevance, not just with what the current system already surfaces. I'd also run an interleaving experiment — randomly interleaving results from the old and new ranking and measuring which individual results users click when both are equally visible, which removes position bias from the comparison entirely since both rankings' results appear at comparable positions across the randomization. If the click-trained model doesn't hold up under either check, that's strong evidence it's reinforcing bias rather than measuring genuine improvement.

**Testing:** whether you can explain the self-reinforcing mechanism of position bias, and propose a genuinely bias-resistant validation method (human judgments, interleaving) rather than just flagging "click data is biased" abstractly.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Validating a click-trained ranker against position bias
